items.title: FortiSandbox Vulnerability Allows Attackers to Access Sensitive Information via Crafted HTTP Requests
items.summary: Fortinet has disclosed a new high-severity vulnerability affecting its FortiSandbox platform , warning that unauthenticated attackers could exploit weaknesses in the product’s web interface to siphon off sensitive information without ever needing valid credentials. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-26084, stems from improper access control in the graphical user interface component that FortiSandbox, FortiSandbox Cloud, and FortiSandbox PaaS all share, and it has been assigned a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.9, placing it firmly in the high-severity category. FortiSandbox is widely deployed across enterprise and government networks as an advanced threat detection appliance, using sandboxing techniques to analyze suspicious files and network traffic for zero-day malware and other advanced threats. FortiSandbox Vulnerability Exposes Sensitive Information According to Fortinet’s advisory , the vulnerability is classified under CWE-284, Improper Access Control. In practical terms, this means the WEB UI fails to properly verify whether a request originates from an authorized session before returning sensitive data. An attacker who understands the structure of the application’s internal API endpoints can craft specially formed HTTP requests and send them directly to the FortiSandbox web interface, bypassing the authentication checks that would normally gate access to that information. The advisory notes that exploitation requires no user interaction and no prior privileges, which is reflected in the CVSS vector’s designation of the attack as unauthenticated. While the vulnerability does not grant an attacker the ability to modify data or execute code, the confidentiality impact is still significant enough to warrant urgent patching, since exposed information from a security appliance like FortiSandbox could include configuration details, logs, or other operational data that attackers could use to plan follow-on intrusions. Fortinet credits Adham El Karn of its own Product Security team with discovering and reporting the issue internally, rather than through an external researcher or bug bounty submission. The company has stated there is no evidence that the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild, and it carries an “Internal” discovery tag along with a “No” rating for known exploitation as of the publication date. FortiSandbox 5.2 is not affected, giving administrators on the latest version extra time to manage it. However, FortiSandbox 5.0 versions from 5.0.0 through 5.0.5 are vulnerable, and Fortinet recommends upgrading to 5.0.6 or later to close the gap. Similarly, FortiSandbox 4.4 versions between 4.4.0 and 4.4.8 are exposed, with 4.4.9 or above serving as the fixed release. The cloud and platform-as-a-service variants show a mixed picture. FortiSandbox Cloud 5.0 is affected in the 5.0.4 through 5.0.5 range, again requiring an upgrade to 5.0.6 or above, while FortiSandbox Cloud 4.4 escapes the issue entirely. On the PaaS side, FortiSandbox PaaS 5.2 is unaffected, but FortiSandbox PaaS 5.0 versions 5.0.4 through 5.0.5 need the same 5.0.6 upgrade path. Product / Deployment Variant Affected Versions Recommended Remediation Severity & Classification FortiSandbox (On-Premises) 5.0.0 through 5.0.5 4.4.0 through 4.4.8 Upgrade to version 5.0.6 or above Upgrade to version 4.4.9 or above High (CVSS 8.9) / CWE-284 Improper Access Control FortiSandbox Cloud 5.0.4 through 5.0.5 Upgrade to version 5.0.6 or above High (CVSS 8.9) / Unauthenticated info disclosure FortiSandbox PaaS 5.0.4 through 5.0.5 Upgrade to version 5.0.6 or above High (CVSS 8.9) / Web UI authentication bypass Unaffected Releases FortiSandbox 5.2, Cloud 4.4, PaaS 5.2 No action required Not vulnerable to CVE-2026-26084 Attackers who gain visibility into sandbox configurations, sample metadata, or internal logs can use that intelligence to evade detection or identify other soft spots in an organization’s infrastructure. This disclosure also fits a broader pattern seen across Fortinet’s product line over the past several months, where multiple FortiSandbox and related appliances have faced scrutiny for authorization weaknesses in their web-based management consoles. Organizations running any vulnerable version of FortiSandbox, FortiSandbox Cloud, or FortiSandbox PaaS should move to the corresponding fixed release without delay. items.title: Book Review: "The Scaling Era"
items.summary: "The Scaling Era: An Oral History of AI, 2019-2025" by Dwarkesh Patel with Gavin Leech, is a riveting conversation among the people who helped create, study, fund, and interpret about frontier AI development. The Scaling Era is an amazing oral history of the AI scaling revolution, from the years 2019-2025. Patel cuts his interviews together across eight subjects: scaling, evals, internals, safety, inputs, impact, intelligence explosion, and timelines. The result feels almost like sitting at a roundtable where people with sharply different rationals keep answering one another indirectly. Underneath the surface of the interviews, it is repeatedly asking questions like, "What actually determines what an intelligent system is, what real progress has been made in the last 6 years, and how far away from AGI are we really?" I listened to the book on Audible at roughly $15 for ~6 hours. Overall I give the book 7 out of 10 stars, and recommend it anyone that is interested in technology history, especially those interested in AI. The book is great because it is so densely packed with information and great interviews, and everyone in the book speaks very fast, so I couldn't imagine listening to this on more than 1x speed. I've even found myself returning to the conversations over time as they have such valuable insights. The following are the chapters of the book, in my typical review style, so you can get a better idea of the narrative journey it takes us on: Preface Chapter 1: Scaling Chapter 2: Evals Chapter 3: Internals Chapter 4: Safety Chapter 5: Inputs Chapter 6: Impact Chapter 7: Explosion Chapter 8: Timelines Conclusion That doesn't really cover the contents of the book though, as it's mostly interviews with tons of AI critical thinkers and builders. The exact interviewee roster in the book's “Profiles” section is 20 people: Dario Amodei, Leopold Aschenbrenner, Gwern Branwen, Trenton Bricken, Joe Carlsmith, François Chollet, Ajeya Cotra, Tyler Cowen, Sholto Douglas, Demis Hassabis, Jared Kaplan, Holden Karnofsky, Shane Legg, Dylan Patel, John Schulman, Carl Shulman, Ilya Sutskever, Jon Y. of Asianometry, Eliezer Yudkowsky, and Mark Zuckerberg. It is also unusually good at moving between levels of abstraction. One minute Jared Kaplan or Dario Amodei is discussing scaling laws; the next Shane Legg is talking about memory and learning; Sholto Douglas about agent reliability; Trenton Bricken about representations; Joe Carlsmith or Eliezer Yudkowsky about goals and control; Dylan Patel about chips and infrastructure; Tyler Cowen about economics. That said, Dwarkesh explicitly acknowledges that many interviewees are founders, developers, researchers, investors, or equity holders who are strongly selected for believing AI will matter enormously. So this is an extraordinary inside view, but not a representative social history of AI. There are comparatively few voices from labor, sociology, education, psychology, public administration, ordinary users, or communities affected by deployment. Still, the interviews contained within are powerful, insightful, and from some of the most "in-the-know" people in the industry.  Also despite the “2019–2025” title, Patel states that the book's knowledge cutoff is November 2024. The book is best treated as a remarkably well-preserved snapshot of what leading participants believed at the end of that scaling era phase, rather than a current account of everything that followed. Some of the best takeaways for me were that while the model supplies a space of possible behavior; the surrounding context, training, memory, tools, incentives, evaluation, and environment greatly influence the set of outcomes the agent ends up selecting. As such, the book is surprisingly relevant to agent architecture, even though it isn't marketed as an agent-design book. The following is an interview with Dwarkesh where he does an overview of this timeline of the Scaling Era, extracting many of the points from the interviews:
